From Roads to Cities, Arms and Cunning

Day breaks over Tharbad. A thick mist blankets the Gwathló, still concealing the banks where the first boatmen are preparing their craft. In the streets near the river, merchants open their warehouses, drivers gather their horses, and the employees of the trading houses check the loads bound for the northern lands.

The city has lost some of the prosperity it once enjoyed, when the kingdoms of Arnor and Gondor maintained regular contact along the great road that linked them. Yet its older buildings remain in view: stone quays, warehouses, paved streets, and structures whose foundations date back several centuries. Travellers still pass through, bringing goods, news, and sometimes affairs they would rather not discuss before the authorities.

In the common room of an inn near the north road, a woman studies the men eating at the surrounding tables. She wears a travelling tunic, a brown leather jerkin, and a cloak whose hem has been mended several times. A short sword rests against the bench beside her, within easy reach. Her chestnut hair is tied back at the nape of her neck, and her face bears the marks of a life spent upon the roads.

Her name is Eraneth. For several years, she has escorted merchant convoys between Tharbad and the settlements of Eriador. She knows the inns, the difficult crossings, and the inhabitants of the villages along the way. Merchants readily entrust her with the protection of their cargoes, for she knows how to wield a weapon and has considerable experience of the negotiations that accompany a journey.

This morning, she is waiting for a man who asked to meet her before his caravan departs.

The merchant arrives shortly after dawn. He looks troubled. During the night, an armed band established a toll post north of the city, on a stretch of road where travellers must slow to cross wet ground. The men claim to act on behalf of a local authority and demand a substantial payment from every convoy.

The merchant tried to reason with them. One of his drivers was struck, and a young boy entrusted with watching the horses was detained until the toll was paid.

Eraneth listens closely. She asks how many men hold the crossing, what weapons they carry, and whether they displayed any documents proving their authority. The merchant hesitates over several details, then admits that the men produced nothing in writing. Their leader wore a cloak fastened with a silver brooch, but his companions appeared to be dressed in a motley assortment of equipment.

The young woman knows this crossing. The customary toll is collected closer to the city, and the authorities responsible for it employ guards whose colours she would recognise.

She proposes to go there with three men.

They leave Tharbad in the middle of the morning. The road runs through low-lying land, where rain has filled the ditches. A few leagues to the north, Eraneth spots a makeshift barrier erected between two ancient milestones. Five armed men stand beside a fire. A sixth watches several horses tethered to a tree. The young driver sits apart, his hands bound.

She tells her companions to remain with the mounts and goes forward alone.

The band's leader comes to meet her. He demands payment of the toll and gestures impatiently towards the barrier. Eraneth studies his brooch, his weapons, and the two men who have approached behind him. On their boots she recognises the reddish mud of a side track leading towards the western hills. The leader also wears a sword whose scabbard appears to belong to an older set of military equipment.

She asks the name of the official responsible for collecting the toll. The man answers confidently, but names an officer whom Eraneth knows to have left Tharbad several years before.

She maintains an attentive expression and continues the conversation. She speaks of the merchants who regularly travel through the region, the city's authorities, and the ledgers in which the money collected ought to be recorded. As the exchange continues, the men begin to glance uneasily at one another.

Their leader loses patience. He suddenly steps closer and places a hand upon his sword.

Eraneth takes one step back, leaving herself enough room to defend herself. When the man tries to seize her, she turns his arm aside and shoves him away with force. He draws his blade. She draws hers in turn and parries the first blow, then takes advantage of an overextended movement to strike him upon the wrist.

The man drops his weapon.

His two companions hesitate. At that same moment, the merchants waiting beside the horses advance along the road, weapons in hand. Eraneth orders the toll collectors to stand back and warns them that a patrol will soon be sent from Tharbad.

Their leader, wounded and taken aback by the resistance he has encountered, finally agrees to leave the road. The men gather their belongings and withdraw towards the hills, abandoning the young driver.

Eraneth has the boy released. She examines his injury, then asks the merchants to make their way back to the city without delay. The armed men might return with reinforcements, and the authorities must be warned before they attack other travellers.

That evening, she returns to the inn's common room. The merchant gives her the agreed sum, along with a few additional coins. He thanks her for preventing a more serious confrontation and invites her to accompany the convoy departing the next day.

Eraneth accepts. The north road is familiar to her, and she knows several families who can shelter the caravan should the rains continue.

Since her youth, she has learned to live among people whose interests do not always coincide. Travel has taught her to recognise lies, garrison life has fostered her skill with weapons, and the markets have shown her the value of patient negotiation.

She can fight, conceal herself, persuade others, and improvise when events no longer follow the expected course.

She is a Rogue, and her experience enables her to resolve difficulties that soldiers, artisans, and scholars might sometimes approach by very different means.

A Life Between Several Trades

In Middle-earth, professions often arise from well-established traditions. Fighters receive training in arms, artisans learn under their masters, and spellcasters devote long years to particular disciplines.

The Rogue follows a more varied path. Her knowledge comes from the occupations she has pursued, the people she has known, and the situations to which she has had to adapt.

Some begin life as soldiers, messengers, or caravan guards. Others work among merchants, sailors, or travellers who regularly cross the frontiers. A few grow up in districts where personal relationships, commerce, and rivalries matter as much as the laws proclaimed by the authorities.

Their training gradually brings together weapons, mobility, observation, and the skills needed to deal with other people. This versatility allows them to approach difficulties from several directions.

A Rogue may escort a caravan, scout a crossing, conduct a negotiation, or intervene when a fight becomes unavoidable. Such a character seldom possesses the martial specialisation of an experienced Fighter or the deep technical expertise of a Thief, but can bring several different abilities to bear upon the demands of a situation.

This calling is particularly well suited to regions where the authorities are distant and inhabitants must frequently rely upon their own resources. The roads of Eriador, the frontier settlements of Gondor, and the southern ports offer abundant opportunities to those who know how to protect their interests without holding an official position.

The Rogue thus acquires a practical understanding of the world. The character learns to recognise the actual responsibilities of those encountered, to understand local customs, and to weigh the consequences of a decision before committing to it.

A Rogue's reputation rests upon the services rendered, the promises kept, and the manner in which those skills are employed.

The Paths of Apprenticeship

Few establishments explicitly teach anyone how to become a Rogue. Most characters acquire their skills from several teachers, often encountered during a life that has already been eventful.

In a port, a young man may begin as an errand-runner. He carries messages between ships and warehouses, accompanies drivers, and gradually learns to recognise captains, merchants, and the men responsible for keeping watch over the quays.

Experience teaches him the customs of trade, the differences between crews, and the circumstances in which a conversation must remain discreet. He also discovers the dangers associated with certain cargoes.

On the roads, apprenticeship takes another form. A young companion travels with an itinerant merchant, cares for the horses, and helps guard the goods. His journeys teach him about inns, fords, and the roads that remain passable during the more difficult seasons.

Training in arms may come from a former soldier or an experienced guard. That mentor teaches him to handle a blade, defend a position, and recognise an opponent's movements. Regular practice gives the future Rogue martial skills sound enough to face the ordinary dangers of travel.

Some receive a more unusual education. A servant in a noble household learns to observe visitors and carry confidential messages. A guide takes part in expeditions through dangerous lands. A sailor learns how to fight on a ship's deck or defend himself in the narrow streets of a harbour.

Over the years, these skills become complementary. The Rogue comes to understand that martial ability can support a difficult negotiation, while an understanding of people can sometimes prevent a fight altogether.

Mistakes play an important part in this education. An ill-considered promise, a misunderstood contract, or trust placed in the wrong person may have lasting consequences. Experience gradually teaches the character to recognise which risks are worth taking and which should be left to others.

The Rogue's Weapons

The Rogue belongs among those professions that receive genuine martial training. Such a character can achieve considerable mastery of weapons, particularly when several years are devoted to a chosen specialisation.

The choice of equipment depends on culture and experience. A former soldier of Gondor may keep his sword and shield, while a sailor from Umbar will favour a blade suited to fighting in confined spaces. A guide from the hills may use an axe and a bow, while a merchant accustomed to travelling may prefer a weapon that is easy to carry.

Mobility generally remains important. The Rogue must be able to move swiftly, overcome obstacles, and retain enough freedom of movement to act in places where heavily equipped fighters would encounter difficulties.

Armour is chosen according to the activities most often undertaken. Light armour suits long marches and discreet movement; heavier protection may be worn when training and circumstances allow.

The Rogue also learns to fight in varied surroundings. A brawl in an inn, an ambush on a narrow road, and a struggle among the cargo on a ship make different demands from those of a pitched battle.

The character knows how to recognise obstacles that restrict an enemy's movement and the passages that offer a favourable position. Some become highly skilled at close-quarters fighting, while others prefer ranged weapons and the ability to change position quickly.

This flexibility is one of the profession's principal martial strengths. It allows the Rogue to act effectively in situations where another combatant's specialised training may not be ideally suited to the terrain.

Reading People

Much of a Rogue's experience rests upon an understanding of human behaviour.

Markets, inns, and garrisons are places where information circulates freely. Travellers exchange news, merchants discuss their affairs, and soldiers describe the difficulties encountered on patrol.

The Rogue learns to listen to such conversations and recognise information that may prove useful.

The character observes how people stand, speak, and respond to questions. An anxious driver frequently glances towards his load; an inexperienced guard may hesitate when required to enforce an order; a merchant familiar with negotiation knows how to advance his interests without immediately revealing the limits he has set himself.

Such signs require careful interpretation. Experience teaches that similar behaviour may spring from very different causes. A silent traveller might be hiding a secret, but could just as easily be exhausted after several days on the road.

The Rogue therefore develops a particular attentiveness to context, seeking to understand a person's habits, their relationships with companions, and the circumstances that may explain their reactions.

Social skills hold an important place in this training. Negotiation, influence, and familiarity with customs help the character obtain information, settle disputes, or persuade another person to cooperate.

Some Rogues are gifted speakers. Others prefer to listen, allowing their interlocutors to reveal what they wish to know little by little.

In either case, their effectiveness rests upon knowledge gained through contact with men and women from many different walks of life.

The Roads and Their Dangers

The roads of Middle-earth link communities whose relationships often depend upon commerce and the exchange of news. Travellers encounter merchants, messengers, soldiers, and families journeying towards a new home.

These journeys present many dangers. Bad weather makes certain crossings impassable, brigands prey upon isolated convoys, and wars may interrupt trade between two regions for months at a time.

The Rogue naturally finds a place among those who must face such difficulties.

Some accompany caravans and help protect their cargoes. Others serve as guides, seek alternative routes, or negotiate passage with communities whose customs differ from those of their employers.

Knowledge of the land is a considerable advantage. A Rogue accustomed to crossing Eriador knows which inns will shelter travellers, which villages can provide supplies, and which passages become treacherous during heavy rains.

In Rhovanion, other forms of knowledge are needed. Settlements may be separated by considerable distances, and relations with local inhabitants play an essential part in the safety of an expedition.

Skills of survival and movement complement this experience. The Rogue can find shelter, recognise a difficult route, or accompany companions through a region where the customary roads have vanished.

The character nevertheless remains a versatile traveller, whose knowledge does not necessarily possess the depth of a Ranger's long training in the watch and care of the wild lands.

The Cities of Middle-earth

Cities offer the Rogue opportunities very different from those encountered upon the roads.

In Minas Tirith, relations among noble families, merchants, officers, and artisans create a world in which information often holds great value. A Rogue may work as a messenger, a trusted agent, or a person charged with settling delicate matters.

In the lower circles of the City, the character knows the markets, the establishments frequented by travellers, and the customs of the guilds. Experience makes it possible to find someone, obtain information, or bring a stranger before an influential acquaintance.

In Pelargir, the activity of the harbour gives the profession a different expression. Ships bring goods and crews from distant lands. Captains seek people who can negotiate, watch over cargo, or defend their interests when a dispute arises.

In Umbar, rivalries between powerful houses and seafaring traditions likewise favour characters who can combine skill at arms with discretion. A Rogue may serve a captain, take part in expeditions, or act as an intermediary in affairs whose stakes extend beyond ordinary trade.

In the smaller settlements of Eriador, personal connections become particularly important. In Bree, a man known to the innkeepers, drivers, and local families may obtain information that an outsider would find very difficult to gather.

Cities thus shape Rogues with different habits. Some develop remarkable social ease, while others become specialists above all in surveillance, movement, or protection.

Relationships and Debts

A Rogue's life often rests upon a web of personal relationships built over many years.

An old companion-in-arms owes the character a favour; a merchant regularly entrusts them with assignments; an innkeeper agrees to pass on messages; a family remembers the help received during a difficult journey.

Such connections are a valuable resource, particularly in regions where the authorities have few means of intervening quickly.

Trust, however, develops over time. A Rogue may be known for honouring every commitment scrupulously or, conversely, have a reputation for abandoning companions when self-interest demands it.

Debts sometimes occupy an important place in the character's existence. They do not always involve money. Someone saved in battle may believe that he now owes assistance to his rescuer. A family that sheltered a traveller through a harsh winter may ask a favour of that person years later.

These obligations may lead the Rogue to accept missions that would otherwise have been refused.

They become especially complex when the interests of several people to whom the character remains loyal come into conflict.

An old companion asks the Rogue to conceal a cargo, while a trusted merchant wants to know its destination. A lord demands information whose disclosure could endanger an entire community.

The Rogue must then decide what value to place upon those commitments and how far to accept their consequences.

Outlaws and Men of the Borderlands

Times of war and unrest encourage the emergence of groups living beyond the reach of established authorities. Some bring together men who have lost their lands, others soldiers deprived of employment or individuals pursued for their deeds.

Tolkien's writings provide a particularly significant example in the Gaurwaith, the outlaws whom Túrin joins after leaving Doriath.

This band brings together men of different backgrounds. Some have been driven from their homes by war; others have committed acts that led them to live among the forests. Under Forweg's leadership, their activities inspire fear among the neighbouring inhabitants.

When Túrin discovers how their leader has treated a young woman, he intervenes and kills Forweg. Having become the leader of the outlaws himself, he attempts to change their conduct and turn their strength against the Orcs.

This episode, recounted notably in The Children of Húrin, shows how the life of an armed band may be shaped by its members' convictions and by the decisions of those who command it.

Túrin is not a Rogue in the mechanical sense of RMU. His story nevertheless offers a striking illustration of irregular companies, their loyalties, and the choices their members may face.

A Rogue may belong to a similar group, but might equally seek to leave it, fight against it, or protect the people endangered by its activities.

The Traditions of Different Peoples

The Rogue profession can be represented among many cultures of Middle-earth.

Among the Dúnedain of Gondor, some characters receive martial training before taking on duties that also demand discretion and social skill. A former soldier may become an escort, an investigator, or a trusted agent of an important household.

Among the Dúnedain of the North, the need to protect scattered communities may encourage characters able to fight, gather information, and travel discreetly. Their training remains distinct from that of Rangers, even where some of their skills overlap.

Among the Dunlendings, the profession may represent a guide, an intermediary between clans, or a fighter accustomed to difficult relations with neighbouring peoples. Knowledge of local customs becomes particularly important where old conflicts still influence trade and other dealings.

The Dorwinrim offer another setting. A Rogue may belong to a merchant family and have developed martial skills over the course of dangerous journeys. Trade with neighbouring regions brings familiarity with languages, goods, and commercial customs.

In Umbar, the traditions of the Corsairs suggest characters able to serve aboard ships while undertaking discreet missions ashore. Relations among captains, merchants, and great families sustain the alliances and rivalries upon which their careers may depend.

Among Hobbits, a Rogue might be a particularly adventurous traveller, accustomed to negotiation, self-defence, and journeys along the roads. The profession is nevertheless less naturally associated with their customary way of life than some of the ordinary occupations practised within their communities.

Among Dwarves, it may represent an itinerant merchant, a convoy guard, or a fighter who has gained varied experience during travels. The traditions of the character's House and obligations towards family still hold an important place in that history.

These different origins give a character different skills, weapons, and responsibilities, while preserving the profession's versatile orientation.

The Rogue and the Thief

The Rogue and the Thief share several skills, particularly in stealth, observation, and subterfuge.

Their training, however, differs in important respects.

The Thief develops expertise in intrusion, mechanisms, locks, and traps. A Thief's effectiveness often rests upon great precision and specialised skills that make it possible to overcome obstacles without drawing attention.

The Rogue follows a more balanced course between arms, movement, and subterfuge. The profession retains particularly favourable martial training and enables its practitioners to act in situations where a difficult negotiation may swiftly turn into a fight.

This difference determines neither a character's morality nor their place in society.

A Thief may work for a city's authorities, while a Rogue may belong to a band of brigands. Both professions are open to loyal, ambitious, cautious, or dishonest characters.

Within an adventuring company, their abilities become complementary. The Thief examines the mechanisms protecting a passage, while the Rogue may keep watch, speak with those who occupy the place, or take an effective part in defending the group.

The distinction should therefore be understood as a difference in training, rather than a rigid separation between two social worlds.

Trusted Agents and Servants of the Powerful

Some Rogues exercise their talents in the service of lords, merchant families, or military commanders.

Their missions may involve protecting a messenger, seeking information, or watching someone whose intentions remain uncertain. In the borderlands, a captain may employ an experienced agent to negotiate the passage of a convoy or investigate a suspicious settlement.

Such duties require considerable discretion. The Rogue may need to appear as an ordinary traveller, join conversations, and gather information without revealing the true purpose of the assignment.

Loyalty to an employer then becomes an important responsibility.

Some patrons honour the commitments they make to their agents. Others regard those agents' services as a means of obtaining results without personally accepting the consequences of the actions undertaken.

An experienced Rogue learns to recognise these differences. The character may agree to serve a powerful master, but generally seeks to understand the interests with which such service will become entangled.

Political rivalries give these missions particular significance. In a city where several families seek control of a trade route, a seemingly minor piece of information may prompt decisions that affect many people.

The profession thus offers opportunities for adventures built around human relationships, trust, and individual responsibility.

Compromises and the Shadow

A Rogue's life often demands choices between competing obligations.

The desire for wealth, safety, or recognition may influence those choices. One character accepts a particularly lucrative mission despite misgivings about its purpose; another conceals information to protect someone dear to them.

Such compromises may become profoundly consequential when the interests of the servants of the Shadow are involved.

In Bree, Bill Ferny provides a particularly telling example of commonplace corruption. He has dealings with the Black Riders and supplies them with information about the Hobbits. Later, he also serves the men who impose Saruman's authority upon the Shire. His conduct shows how self-interest and opportunism may lead someone to support powers whose purposes extend far beyond the advantages he hopes to gain.

Bill Ferny is not a mechanical model for the Rogue profession. He nevertheless illustrates the dangers associated with certain forms of clandestine collaboration.

Other characters may use similar skills to protect the Free Peoples. A messenger carries information despite enemy surveillance; a former soldier agrees to conceal fugitives; a companion infiltrates a hostile group to discover its intentions.

The Rogue remains responsible for the decisions made and for the consequences of those commitments.

Versatility often provides the character with several possible courses of action. The choices made in employing them determine the part the Rogue plays in the struggle against the Shadow.

The Rogue Through the Ages

The profession has a place in different ages of Middle-earth, but its activities depend profoundly upon the societies and conflicts that characterise each period.

In the First Age, the wars of Beleriand and the migrations of human peoples create circumstances in which fighters must acquire a broad range of skills. A Rogue may belong to an irregular company, accompany travellers, or undertake reconnaissance missions between threatened communities. The story of the Gaurwaith offers a literary example of groups whose existence is shaped by the consequences of war.

In the Second Age, the growth of Númenor and its settlements in Middle-earth encourages commerce, seafaring expeditions, and missions entrusted to reliable agents. Political rivalries and the growing influence of Sauron may also lend considerable importance to those able to gather information and move between communities.

In the Third Age, the profession takes many forms. The ports of Gondor, the settlements of Umbar, the roads of Eriador, and the lands of Rhovanion all offer varied opportunities. The wars against Angmar, followed by the conflicts between Gondor and the forces of Sauron, give agents, messengers, and irregular fighters an important role.

In the Fourth Age, the restoration of the Reunited Kingdom gradually transforms relations between the regions. Roads regain some of their safety, trade expands, and old rivalries may give way to new agreements. A Rogue may accompany expeditions, help protect convoys, or serve as an intermediary between communities whose ties have long been severed.

Each Age thus gives a different meaning to the character's training. The knowledge a Rogue possesses remains closely bound to the activities and responsibilities of the surrounding world.

Leaving Familiar Roads

A Rogue often has considerable experience of travel before joining an adventuring company. Such a character knows the roads, the inns, and the ordinary dangers that travellers encounter.

The departure, however, sometimes has more personal causes.

An old companion has disappeared, an important debt must be repaid, or a promise made years earlier leads the character to a distant region. Some seek to leave a city where their activities have earned them enemies. Others wish to discover lands they know only from travellers' tales.

The adventuring life allows the Rogue to employ familiar skills in new circumstances. The character accompanies companions on their journeys, takes part in fighting, and contributes knowledge whenever negotiation or investigation becomes necessary.

The variety of these talents gives the Rogue a particularly flexible role within the group. The character may support a Fighter in battle, help a Ranger watch a passage, or accompany a Thief on an assignment requiring stealth.

Yet versatility also demands an understanding of those fields in which others possess deeper training.

A Rogue accustomed to commercial negotiations may discover that a Lay Healer better understands the consequences of a serious injury. An experienced scout on the roads may meet an Animist whose knowledge of animals and plants greatly exceeds their own.

Such exchanges enrich the Rogue's experience and allow certain skills to be developed further without abandoning the general character of the profession.

As journeys succeed one another, relationships with companions may become more important than the obligations upon which the Rogue once depended for a living. A character accustomed to bargaining over every service may discover the value of loyalty that expects no reward.

Playing a Rogue

The Rogue offers the opportunity to portray a character whose life has been shaped by varied experiences, often acquired among roads, cities, and the people who inhabit them.

A former soldier of Gondor may have become a caravan guard after leaving his regiment. A young woman from Pelargir may have learned commerce from her family before developing her martial abilities on dangerous journeys. A Dunlending guide knows the hill paths and the rivalries between neighbouring communities. An adventurer from Dorwinion may have remarkable experience of negotiation and trade with other peoples.

The character's relationships with former companions form an important part of this history. Who first taught the Rogue to handle weapons? From whom did the character learn the customs of merchants or the methods of travellers? Is there a debt to repay or a promise whose fulfilment remains difficult?

A Rogue's character may be shaped by the many circles in which they have moved. Some become adept at speaking with strangers and understanding their concerns. Others grow particularly wary, accustomed to recognising situations in which people conceal their intentions.

Success may encourage boldness, sometimes to the point of recklessness. A character who has often escaped difficulties through quick thinking may underestimate unfamiliar dangers. Conversely, one who has suffered betrayal may hesitate to trust even companions whose loyalty has been proved.

The profession is particularly suitable for campaigns in which characters travel between diverse communities, take part in negotiations, and face dangers demanding more than a single kind of skill.

A Rogue may become a loyal companion, an ambitious adventurer, a former smuggler seeking a new life, or a trusted agent whose obligations draw them into events beyond anything they had foreseen.

Over the course of life, the character will discover that adaptability is a considerable strength. Yet the choices to which the Rogue remains faithful, particularly when the interests of companions conflict with personal interests, will give those talents their true meaning.

Gamemaster's Notes — The Rogue in MERP-RMU

The Rogue is a non-spell user whose training combines martial skills, movement, subterfuge, and practical abilities.

Prime Stats

The Rogue's prime stats are:

• Agility (Ag), which supports precise movements, mobility, and skills of subterfuge;

• Strength (St), which reflects the profession's genuine martial orientation.

These two stats correspond to the profile adopted in MERP-UI.

Professional skills include, in particular, Riding, Awareness, Armour Manoeuvring, Restricted Quarters Combat, Blind Fighting, Body Development, Survival, Jumping, Climbing, Running, Ambush, Stalking, and certain specialised fields of knowledge, including Poison Mastery.

These skills reflect the character's development options and imply neither any particular practice nor any moral obligation.

No Base Spell Lists

The Rogue has no professional Base Spell Lists.

Any potential access to magic remains subject to RMU's general mechanisms, development costs, and the cultural restrictions applicable in MERP-RMU.

The profession is founded primarily upon acquired skills and experience.

Rogue, Fighter, and Thief

The Fighter benefits from more extensive training in the various martial techniques and forms of protection.

The Thief possesses a stronger specialisation in intrusion, mechanisms, and clandestine activities.

The Rogue combines genuine martial ability with favourable costs in Movement, Subterfuge, and Awareness.

These differences make it possible to represent several characters from the same culture who have followed distinct paths of training.

Literary Inspirations

Tolkien's writings offer many inspirations for irregular companies, discreet agents, and characters able to act outside established military organisations.

The Gaurwaith, the clandestine activities of certain servants of the Shadow, and the adventures of travellers confronting unexpected difficulties all provide interesting situations.

Such characters should not, however, automatically be equated with the Rogue profession as mechanically defined.

Shadow and Corruption

The profession has no intrinsic association with the Shadow.

The risks of Corruption depend upon the character's actions, the commitments accepted, and the circumstances provided for in MERP-RMU.

Cunning, concealment, and negotiation are not, in themselves, manifestations of Corruption. Their moral significance depends upon how they are employed and upon the consequences for the people concerned.

The Rogue comes fully into their own when their skills enable them to act with flexibility, protect their companions, and make decisions in situations where several interests meet.
